passages.t: A heavy yoke, and two kinds of advice
passages.happening:
Rehoboam goes to Shechem, ‘for all Israel had gone there to make him king’ (verse 1). Jeroboam is called back from Egypt, and he and the whole assembly come to Rehoboam: “Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you should lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you” (verse 4). Rehoboam asks for three days.

He asks the elders who had served Solomon, and they answer, “If you will be a servant to these people and serve them this day, and if you will respond by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever” (verse 7). Then he asks the young men who grew up with him. They tell him to boast that his little finger is thicker than his father's waist, and to promise a heavier yoke (verses 10-11).

On the third day ‘the king answered the people harshly’ (verse 13). He says, “Whereas my father made your yoke heavy, I will add to your yoke. Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions” (verse 14). ‘So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from the LORD, to fulfill the word He had spoken to Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah the Shilonite’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The northern tribes come to Shechem, the old place where Joshua had renewed Israel's covenant, to make a king. Their coming suggests that for them kingship was something agreed, with conditions, and not simply inherited. Israel and Judah had been crowned separately in David's time, and the seam between them was old.

Their request is put in the language of service: lighten the yoke, and they will serve the king. A yoke was the beam that bound an animal to its work, and it was a common picture of a ruler's demands. Solomon's taxes and labor levy, organized by districts in chapter 4, had fallen heavily on the north.

The elders' answer is a small picture of the good ruler: serve the people, and they will serve you. The young men's reply is crude bravado; the word translated waist is a coarse image, and scorpions probably means whips fitted with barbs or spikes. The word advice runs through the scene. Solomon's son had good counsel within reach and chose the advice that flattered him. Wisdom, it turns out, was not inherited.

Verse 15 steps back and names God's hand in the event. Ahijah's word of chapter 11 comes true through a young king's pride.
passages.later: Proverbs says it in a line: ‘A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger’ (Proverbs 15:1).
passages.hard:
If the split was from the LORD (verse 15), was Rehoboam responsible for it?

The text says both things. Rehoboam made a free and foolish choice, rejecting good advice for bad, and the narrator gives no sign that he was forced. At the same time the event fulfilled what God had announced through Ahijah as judgment on Solomon's idolatry.

Christian interpreters explain this in different ways. Some stress God's governing providence, in which he ordains events that include human choices. Others stress God's foreknowledge and his use of human sin to bring about a just judgment. Nearly all agree that the Bible never lets God's rule cancel human responsibility, or makes God the author of evil. Rehoboam answers for his harshness, and God is at work in it.
passages.asks: Rehoboam had wise counsel and chose the voices that flattered him. Ask whom you listen to when you have power over others. And ask whether you are adding to someone's yoke when you could lighten it.

passages.happening:
When all Israel sees that the king will not listen, they answer him, “What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse? To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, O David!” (verse 16). They go home, and Rehoboam reigns only over the Israelites living in the towns of Judah (verse 17).

Rehoboam sends out Adoram, the man in charge of the forced labor, ‘but all Israel stoned him to death’ (verse 18), and the king escapes to Jerusalem in his chariot. “So to this day Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David” (verse 19). The north makes Jeroboam king over all Israel, and only the tribe of Judah follows David's house (verse 20).

Rehoboam gathers the men of Judah and Benjamin to fight and win back the kingdom (verse 21). But the word of God comes to Shemaiah, the man of God: ‘You are not to go up and fight against your brothers, the Israelites’ (verse 24). ‘So they listened to the word of the LORD and turned back according to the word of the LORD’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The cry of verse 16 repeats almost word for word the rallying cry of Sheba's revolt against David in 2 Samuel. The north's grievance was old, and Rehoboam gave it its moment.

Sending Adoram was the worst choice possible. He was in charge of the very forced labor the people had complained of, and his death says what they thought of it.

From here until the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, the Bible tells the story of two kingdoms. Israel in the north, often called Ephraim or later Samaria, has ten tribes and a series of dynasties. Judah in the south, with Benjamin, keeps Jerusalem, the temple and David's line. The division is usually dated to about 931 or 930 BC.

The last scene is easy to pass over. A prophet tells a king not to go to war against his brothers, and the king and the people listen. For once in this chapter, someone hears.
passages.later: Sheba had raised the same cry against David: “We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!” (2 Samuel 20:1).
passages.asks: Judah's army turned back because a man of God said these were their brothers. Ask whom you have come to treat as an enemy who is still your brother or sister. And ask what quarrel you could still turn back from because God has spoken.

passages.happening:
Jeroboam builds up Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Penuel across the Jordan (verse 25). Then he says in his heart that if the people keep going up to offer sacrifices at the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, ‘their hearts will return to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah’ (verse 27), and they will kill him.

So he makes two golden calves and tells the people, “Going up to Jerusalem is too much for you. Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (verse 28). “One calf he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan” (verse 29). ‘And this thing became a sin’ (verse 30), and the people walk as far as Dan to worship.

He builds shrines on the high places and appoints priests who are not Levites (verse 31). He sets up a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, ‘a month of his own choosing’ (verse 33), and offers sacrifices and burns incense on the altar he made at Bethel (verses 32-33).
passages.hearers:
The second story, like the first, is about a king making a bad choice out of fear or pride. It opens with Jeroboam speaking in his heart, which lets the reader see that his religious plan springs from political fear.

The bull or young calf was a common sign of strength and fertility in Canaanite and Egyptian religion, and gods such as Baal were sometimes pictured standing on bulls. Many scholars think Jeroboam meant his calves as pedestals for the invisible LORD, a northern match for the cherubim in Jerusalem, rather than images of another god. The text judges them as idols all the same, and Jeroboam's words echo Aaron's words over the golden calf at Sinai.

Bethel lay near the southern border of the new kingdom and had been holy since Jacob's dream there. Dan lay at the far north. At Tel Dan the excavator Avraham Biran uncovered a large raised platform that many archaeologists connect with the northern kingdom's royal sanctuary, though its phases and dates are debated.

His feast in the eighth month shadowed the Feast of Booths held in the seventh month in Judah, and his priests broke the law's rule that priests come from the tribe of Levi. ‘A month of his own choosing’ sums up his whole religion: worship devised by the king, not received from God. Almost every later king of the north is judged by one measure, whether he walked in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat.
passages.later:
Aaron had said the same words at Sinai: “These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” (Exodus 32:4).

Two centuries later the priest of Bethel told the prophet Amos, “But never prophesy at Bethel again, because it is the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom” (Amos 7:13). Hosea said of the calf, ‘a craftsman made it, and it is not God’ (Hosea 8:6).
passages.asks: Jeroboam did not leave the LORD by name; he reshaped worship to keep himself safe. Ask where your faith has been arranged around your own security. And ask what you do in God's name that is of your own choosing.
